桑薩屬體鳴樂器中的舌片琴，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 122.1，傳: The sanza is a lamellaphone within the idiophones, Hornbostel-Sachs number 122.1, and is traditionally associated with the Shona people of Zimbabwe. The sources state that its basic construction is a wooden board set with staggered metal tines or springs, plucked with the hand to sound; some boards are often fitted with a resonator, but the materials of the resonator and the other parts are not described. The historical sources also mention that the tines were once made of bamboo and that metal keys were developed later, so the materials that can be confirmed are mainly wood, metal and bamboo; the rest of the components are not recorded.
桑薩音色清脆明亮，帶有溫潤的金屬質感與輕盈的木質共鳴。其音域通常跨越中音至高音區: The sanza's timbre is crisp and bright, with a warm metallic quality and a light wooden resonance. Its range usually runs from the middle to the high register, and its notes are laid out in a scale of their own. When the fingers pluck the metal or bamboo tines the sound is as clear as beads dropped on jade, and it carries elegantly. The resonator amplifies the faintest vibration and shapes overtones with warmth. Next to the harp the sanza is drier and more direct; next to the xylophone it keeps more of the softness of its harmonics. Its sound lies between percussion and plucked strings: it has the plain, raw quality of a traditional African instrument, and at the same time a clear, modern sound.
桑薩（Sanza）又稱姆比拉、卡林巴或贊扎，是源自辛巴威紹納人的非洲體鳴樂器，H: The sanza (Sanza), also called mbira, kalimba or zanza, is an African idiophone from the Shona people of Zimbabwe, H-S number 122.1, in the lamellaphone / plucked idiophone family. It is built as a wooden board, often with a resonator, set with staggered metal tines; the player holds the instrument in both hands and plucks the tines with thumb and index finger. In eastern and southern Africa it is often found at religious ceremonies, weddings and social gatherings, usually with hosho percussion accompaniment. In the late 1950s the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey made it a commercial product.

The sanza (Sanza), also called mbira, kalimba or zanza, is an African idiophone from the Shona people of Zimbabwe, H-S number 122.1, in the lamellaphone / plucked idiophone family. It is built as a wooden board, often with a resonator, set with staggered metal tines; the player holds the instrument in both hands and plucks the tines with thumb and index finger. In eastern and southern Africa it is often found at religious ceremonies, weddings and social gatherings, usually with hosho percussion accompaniment. In the late 1950s, after the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey made it a commercial product, it became popular outside Africa, and in the West it is usually called the kalimba. In 2020 the art of making and playing the mbira / sanza in Malawi and Zimbabwe was added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
桑薩（姆比拉、卡林巴）常見於紹納人的宗教儀式、婚禮與社交聚會，東南部非洲亦常以霍: The sanza (mbira, kalimba) is often found at Shona religious ceremonies, weddings and social gatherings, and in south-eastern Africa it is usually accompanied by hosho percussion. The traditional piece 'Nhema Musasa' plucks the metal tines with thumb and fingers and builds a cross-rhythm; on the modern stage the instrument is used alongside rock line-ups of electric guitar, bass, drum kit and horns. There are also mbira ensembles in seven tunings, which shows that it can serve as a solo instrument, as accompaniment, or in an ensemble.
演奏桑薩時，以雙手持琴，用拇指或手指撥動木製琴板上的金屬舌片發聲。初學可先熟悉舌: When you play the sanza, hold it in both hands and pluck the metal tines on the wooden board with the thumb or fingers. Begin by getting to know the layout of the tines: the lowest note is usually in the centre and the higher notes lie to left and right, so that the thumb can turn and reach every tine. In practice, keep a steady bass note with the left hand and play the melody above with the right, and notice that the overtones are strongest at the moment of plucking and then settle towards a nearly pure tone. This kind of instrument is a lamellaphone / plucked idiophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 122.1, common in Africa and especially among the Shona of Zimbabwe.
舌片琴在非洲存在數千年，西非海岸約三千年前有木竹舌片樂器，贊比西河谷約一千三百年: Plucked lamellophones have existed in Africa for thousands of years: wood and bamboo tine instruments existed on the west coast of Africa about three thousand years ago, and metal-tined instruments appeared in the Zambezi valley about one thousand three hundred years ago, later spreading across the continent and developing many forms and social uses among the Shona of Zimbabwe. A similar instrument also existed at Okpuje, a village in the Nsukka area of south-eastern Nigeria, in the early twentieth century. In the late 1950s Hugh Tracey designed the kalimba on the model of the nyunga nyunga mbira and exported it commercially, which made it popular outside Africa; in the 1960s and 1970s musicians such as Maurice White and Thomas Mapfumo spread it further by putting it on stage with modern rock instruments. In 2020 the art of making and playing the mbira / sanza in Malawi and Zimbabwe was added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
